claims.statement: A model response is one observation from a configured system, not proof of dependable product behavior.
Evaluation must be designed into development because model outputs and versions can vary.
Technical controls and documentation do not transfer formal risk or domain authority to the LLM engineer.
Success criteria should specify task, inputs, outputs, failure behavior, consequence, and judgment method before model optimization.
Representative language and consequence segments are required because aggregate performance can hide important failures.
Human review is a designed authority and control relationship, not a generic safety guarantee.
Transformer generation conditions each next token on represented prior context through attention-based layers.
Subword tokenization changes sequence length and representation, with language-specific and domain-specific effects.
Decoding and chat-template configuration are part of behavior identity and must be versioned.
Public benchmark or scale alone cannot establish fitness for a specific task and deployment posture.
Managed and weight-access paths expose different control, inspection, hosting, adaptation, and operational surfaces.
Model lifecycle/deprecation risk should be treated as an architecture input before release.
A reproducible behavior baseline identifies model, prompt/messages, context, decoding, schema, evaluator, and runtime configuration.
Repeated trials are needed when stochastic behavior can affect the decision.
A deterministic test double verifies software contracts but cannot establish live-model quality.
Instructions, examples, delimiters, message roles, and templates are configuration surfaces whose effects must be evaluated.
Untrusted retrieved or user content can carry indirect instructions that conflict with application intent.
Prompt instructions alone are not evidence of an effective security or safety control.
Schema-constrained generation can improve syntactic conformance to supported JSON Schema.
Syntactic validity does not establish factual correctness, permission, provenance, or authorization.
Abstention, escalation, repair, and fail-closed behavior should be explicit product states rather than improvised prose.
Context-window capacity does not guarantee equal or reliable use of information at every position.
Longer context can increase input cost and latency, so selection and caching choices require workload measurement.
Truncation, conflict, staleness, and authorization are distinct context failure states.
Retrieval is justified only when external evidence ownership, freshness, or coverage materially improves the task.
Relevance does not establish source authority, permission, currency, or answerability.
A retrieval-grounded system needs independent retrieval and generated-behavior claims.
Sparse, dense, and late-interaction retrieval expose different effectiveness and resource tradeoffs.
Chunking, metadata filters, candidate retrieval, and reranking are separately diagnosable stages.
Synthetic hypothetical-document retrieval is an experimental option, not a truth or grounding guarantee.
Retrieved evidence should retain source identity and citation targets through context assembly.
Supporting, conflicting, stale, absent, and unauthorized evidence require different behavior.
Context ordering and position can affect use, so packing policy needs direct evaluation.
End-to-end RAG quality can fail at corpus, query, retrieval, ranking, context, generation, citation, or evaluation layers.
Retrieval metrics and generated-answer metrics answer different questions and should not be collapsed prematurely.
Groundedness or faithfulness metrics do not prove source truth or organizational authority.
Evaluation cases need documented provenance, segments, coverage, exclusions, split identity, and refresh policy.
Duplicate or contaminated cases can inflate apparent generalization and invalidate comparisons.
Multilingual coverage requires direct per-language/task evidence rather than an English aggregate.
Criteria, error category, consequence, severity, detectability, segment, and disposition are distinct evaluation fields.
LLM judges can exhibit position, verbosity, and self-preference biases.
Model graders should be calibrated against credible human or domain judgments and retain disagreement/limitations.
A causal model-system claim needs a baseline, explicit hypothesis, controlled variable family, repeated trials where relevant, and decision criteria.
Aggregate gains should not erase segment regressions or uncertainty.
An experiment should end in retain, revise, reject, scope, or release disposition rather than score collection alone.
